entries.question: What angered God so much that he didn't allow Moses to enter the promised land?
entries.summary: Numbers 20:7-12 says YHWH barred Moses and Aaron from the promised land because Moses struck the rock at Meribah twice instead of speaking to it as commanded — failing to sanctify YHWH before the people. But Deuteronomy 3:26-27 and 4:21 have Moses tell Israel YHWH was angry with him "for your sakes" — that is, because of the people's sin, not Moses'.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization is the both-and reading: Moses was punished for his own failure at Meribah AND that failure happened in the context of the people's provocation, so Deuteronomy's "for your sakes" language can mean "because of the situation you put me in." Eugene Merrill in his NAC Deuteronomy and Daniel Block in his NIVAC Deuteronomy both run this line. The rebellious complaining of the people in Numbers 20:2-5 is what set up the Meribah incident, so Moses can plausibly say later that the people's behavior contributed to his loss. Gleason Archer in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties takes a similar tack.

This harmonization works at a high level. Deuteronomy 32:51 (in the same book, in the Song of Moses) does explicitly say Moses transgressed against YHWH at Meribah, so Deuteronomy itself doesn't deny Moses' personal failure. And the Hebrew bigelalkem in Deuteronomy 3:26 ("on your account" or "for your sakes") can plausibly mean "because of the situation you produced." So the plain-reading apparent contradiction softens once you read Deuteronomy as a whole rather than just the 3:26 verse in isolation.

Where the harmonization gets weaker is the rhetorical force of Deuteronomy 3:23-27 in context. Moses is recounting his pleading with YHWH and explicitly says "the LORD was wroth with me for your sakes, and would not hear me." The whole rhetorical move is to deflect responsibility outward — to the people — not to confess his own failure. Deuteronomic Moses casts himself as the long-suffering leader bearing the consequences of the congregation's sin, which is in tension with the Numbers 20 portrait of a Moses who fails at the moment of testing. Source critics like Joel Baden and Thomas Dozeman argue the two passages reflect different traditions about why Moses didn't enter the land. The Priestly Numbers tradition needs to explain why even Moses fell short by giving him a specific covenant infraction (cf. similar concerns about Aaron's golden-calf failure in another Priestly handling). The Deuteronomic tradition, focused on the people's recurring rebellion as the great theological theme, attributes Moses' loss to the same pattern of communal disobedience.

There's also a deeper exegetical question about what exactly Moses did wrong at Meribah. The text says "because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel," which is vague. Did he strike instead of speak? Did he say "must we fetch you water" attributing the miracle to himself? Did he show anger rather than faith? Jacob Milgrom in his JPS Numbers catalogues the rabbinic options and notes the text doesn't actually specify. So Numbers 20 itself is somewhat ambiguous about the offense, which makes the comparison with Deuteronomy all the more strained.

Verdict: moderate contradiction. The both-and harmonization is textually defensible if you grant that bigelalkem is broad enough to absorb Moses' own failure. The source-critical evidence points to two different traditions with different theological emphases — Priestly individual-failure versus Deuteronomic communal-failure — assembled side by side without full reconciliation.

entries.question: Where did Aaron die?
entries.summary: Numbers locates Aaron's death and burial at the top of Mount Hor, with Eleazar dressed in the high-priestly garments at the summit. Deuteronomy 10:6 says Aaron died and was buried at Moserah, after the Israelites traveled there from Beeroth Bene-jaakan. The two traditions name two different places.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic move here, going back to Keil & Delitzsch and reproduced almost verbatim in Gleason Archer's *Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties*, is to claim Mount Hor and Moserah are the same location, or at least that Moserah was a station at the foot of Mount Hor. Archer suggests the Deuteronomist is just naming the regional staging area while Numbers names the peak. Hard to falsify, easy to assert. That's the strongest version of the harmonization, and you can find it copy-pasted across apologetics sites.

The problem is the itineraries don't cooperate. Numbers 33:31-38 gives a detailed wilderness travel log, and in that list Moseroth and Mount Hor are separated by seven encampments — Bene-jaakan, Hor-haggidgad, Jotbathah, Abronah, Ezion-geber, Kadesh, then finally Mount Hor. Deuteronomy 10:6 reverses the direction of travel (from Bene-jaakan to Moserah, not Moserah to Bene-jaakan, as in Numbers) and collapses Aaron's death into Moserah itself. This isn't a regional vs. peak distinction. It's two different itineraries placing the death at two different stops.

The critical-scholarship read is straightforward. The Numbers material is from the Priestly source, which has a strong vested interest in Aaron's death scene because it's where the priesthood transfers to Eleazar — the whole vestment-stripping ceremony in Numbers 20:28 is P's investiture liturgy in narrative form. Deuteronomy 10:6-7 reflects an older or independent itinerary tradition that didn't know or didn't care about the P version. Martin Noth flagged the Deuteronomy passage as an awkward intrusion into Moses' speech precisely because it contradicts the Numbers itinerary. Jacob Milgrom, in the JPS Torah Commentary on Numbers, treats P's Mount Hor account as a deliberate cultic etiology rather than a geographical report.

You can squeeze the texts into harmony if you assume Moserah is shorthand for the Hor region and ignore the seven intervening stations in Numbers 33. Or you can read the texts as they actually are: two source traditions disagreeing about where Aaron died. Genuine contradiction.

entries.question: Did Balaam curse the Israelites?
entries.summary: Numbers 23-24 tells the story straight: Balaam was hired to curse Israel, but each time he opened his mouth God forced blessings out instead. Balak fumes that he hired Balaam to curse and got blessings three times. Deuteronomy 23:3-4, however, justifies the permanent exclusion of Moabites and Ammonites by declaring that they hired Balaam to curse Israel — implying the cursing was actual.
entries.commentary:
Apologists like Archer and Walter Kaiser handle this by reading Deuteronomy 23:4 as a reference to the *attempt* or the *intent* to curse, not the successful execution. The Hebrew verb *qalal* in the infinitive can describe a commission rather than a completed act, so the argument goes: Moab hired Balaam *for the purpose* of cursing, even though the cursing failed. The NIV essentially translates it that way. That's the strongest harmonization on offer and it's grammatically defensible.

But the way Deuteronomy actually frames the offense is the problem. Deuteronomy 23:3-6 stacks the indictment: Moab and Ammon didn't meet you with bread and water, AND they hired Balaam to curse you. The accusation is parallel — these are both real, completed wrongs done to Israel that justify generational exclusion. Reading verse 4 as merely intent while verse 4a is a real failure to provide hospitality requires you to flip register mid-verse for harmonization purposes. The passage continues, 'Nevertheless the LORD your God would not listen to Balaam; the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you.' The Deuteronomist clearly believes a curse was uttered and Yahweh transformed it. That's not the Numbers picture, where Balaam is forced from the start to bless rather than curse.

More importantly, Deuteronomy 23 attributes the hiring to the Ammonites as well as the Moabites — Numbers only knows about Balak the Moabite. So we already have the Deuteronomist working with a different version of the tradition. Thomas Dozeman treats the Balaam cycle in Numbers 22-24 as a complex composite (the famous talking-donkey scene in Numbers 22 sits in tension with the surrounding poetry, and the oracles themselves are widely considered older independent material). The Deuteronomic redactor working centuries later has reshaped the Balaam memory into something Numbers wouldn't recognize.

The harmonization works only if you accept that 'curse' in Deuteronomy 23:4 means 'tried to curse' even though the parallel offenses in the same passage are completed actions. That's special pleading. Genuine contradiction at the level of the surface narrative, even if mild on the deeper redactional reading.

entries.question: Does God lie?
entries.books_in_tension: Numbers, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Psalms, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, 2 Thessalonians, Titus, Hebrews
entries.summary: Numbers 23:19, 1 Samuel 15:29, Titus 1:2, and Hebrews 6:18 declare flatly that God cannot lie. Yet 1 Kings 22:23 has Yahweh personally putting a 'lying spirit' in the mouth of Ahab's prophets to lure him to his death, Ezekiel 14:9 has God say 'if a prophet is deceived, I the LORD have deceived that prophet,' and 2 Thessalonians 2:11 has God sending strong delusion so that people will believe a lie. The 'cannot lie' verses and the 'God deceives' verses can't both stand without redefinition.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization — you'll find it in Geisler & Howe's *When Critics Ask*, in Norman Geisler's *Systematic Theology*, and dressed up in Reformed dress in John Frame — is to distinguish between God *directly* lying (which He cannot do, by nature) and God *judicially* sending deception as punishment for those who have already rejected truth. The lying spirit in 1 Kings 22 isn't God lying; it's God permitting or commissioning a deceiving spirit to enact judgment on a king who has already chosen unrighteousness. Ezekiel 14:9 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11 get the same treatment — judicial hardening, not divine mendacity. That's the strongest harmonization and it has a long pedigree going back to Augustine and Aquinas on the *concursus* problem.

But look at how these verses actually phrase it. 1 Kings 22:22 has Yahweh in the divine council asking 'Who will entice Ahab?' and accepting the volunteer spirit's plan: 'I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' Yahweh replies, 'You shall entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.' Yahweh isn't permitting deception, He's commissioning it. Ezekiel 14:9 is even more direct: 'I the LORD have deceived that prophet' — *pittiti*, the piel of the verb meaning to seduce or deceive. The text gives Yahweh the active verb. 2 Thessalonians 2:11 has God *sending* (*pempei*) the strong delusion. These aren't permissive constructions in the Greek or Hebrew. They're causative.

More fundamentally, the 'cannot lie' verses are theological assertions developed in late strata — Titus 1:2 and Hebrews 6:18 are post-Pauline texts working out a Hellenistic philosophical concept of divine immutability, where the Greek god of the philosophers cannot be subject to change or deception. James Crenshaw and Walter Brueggemann have written extensively about how the Hebrew Bible's older deity is much more comfortable with deception as a tool of judgment — 1 Kings 22 sits inside a worldview where the divine council can plot. The 'God cannot lie' theology is a later philosophical overlay onto a text that includes the older, messier picture. Calling 1 Kings 22 'judicial deception that doesn't count as lying' is exactly the kind of post-hoc rationalization the apologist playbook runs on.

The harmonization works only if you redefine 'lie' so narrowly that 'I have deceived that prophet' doesn't qualify. Take your pick: either God doesn't lie and Ezekiel was confused, or God does deceive and Titus is wrong. Genuine contradiction, and it's one of the cleaner ones in the database.

entries.question: How many did God kill for committing whoredom with the daughters of Moab?
entries.summary: Numbers 25:9 puts the death toll from the Baal-Peor plague at 24,000. Paul, citing the same incident in 1 Corinthians 10:8, says 23,000 fell in one day. The numbers don't match.
entries.commentary:
Apologists from Archer to Calvin have offered roughly two harmonizations. First: Paul says 'in one day' — maybe 23,000 died on the first day and the additional 1,000 trickled in afterward, bringing the Numbers total to 24,000. Second: Paul is rounding, or possibly conflating with another plague. Archer goes with the first option, treating 23,000 as a one-day subtotal of the larger 24,000 final body count. That's the strongest harmonization on the table.

The first move is plausible enough on its face but it requires inserting a detail Paul doesn't actually provide. Numbers 25:9 says simply, 'those that died in the plague were 24,000' — there's no time qualifier and no hint that 23,000 was a one-day subset. Paul, on the other hand, is not paraphrasing Numbers carefully. He's working from memory or from a homiletic tradition. Early Jewish exegetical sources engage the Baal-Peor plague figure (Sifre Numbers §131; y. Sanhedrin 10:2), and there's evidence that Hellenistic Jewish midrashic traditions varied in how they reported it. Joseph Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible Corinthians commentary notes the discrepancy and treats Paul as drawing on a tradition that already had a different number, not as carefully harmonizing with Numbers.

There's also a textual-critical wrinkle worth flagging. The Septuagint of Numbers 25:9 reads 24,000 (matching the MT), but some early Christian writers, including some Greek manuscripts, attempted to harmonize Paul's number with the LXX. The variant tradition shows that ancient scribes themselves noticed the problem and tried to fix it. That's the textual fingerprint of a real contradiction, not an apparent one. If it were obvious that Paul meant a one-day subset, no scribe would have needed to harmonize anything.

The harmonization is possible. It's also unfalsifiable — you can always insert 'maybe Paul meant only the first day's count' to rescue the numbers. But the most parsimonious read is that Paul is loosely citing a tradition that gave a different number than Numbers, and the discrepancy is real. Mild contradiction at the surface level, completely explicable on a critical reading where Paul isn't a flawless transcriber of Hebrew Bible casualty figures.

entries.question: Did God burn all of Korah's children to death?
entries.summary: Numbers 16:27-33 describes the earth opening and swallowing Korah, Dathan, Abiram, their wives, sons, and little children, with the families perishing alive. Numbers 26:11 then says, in passing, 'Notwithstanding the children of Korah died not.' Either Korah's children went down into the pit with him or they didn't.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic move — Archer, Keil & Delitzsch, and most evangelical commentaries — is to argue that Numbers 16 only describes the deaths of those physically present at the rebellion, and that Korah's adult sons (those who became the famous Korahite singers later in 1 Chronicles and the psalm superscriptions) were not present at their father's mutiny. The rebels' households perished, but Korah's own sons either dissented from his rebellion or were not in his tent at the moment of judgment. That's the harmonization, and it has the virtue of preserving the later Korahite Levitical lineage, which the Chronicler clearly treats as legitimate.

The problem is that Numbers 16:27 is explicit about *Korah's* household: it lists Korah, Dathan, and Abiram as standing 'in the door of their tents, and their wives, and their sons, and their little children.' Verse 32 says the earth swallowed 'all the men that pertained unto Korah and all their goods.' The text is structured to show comprehensive judgment on the entire rebel household. To rescue Korahite descendants, you have to assume Korah's sons happened to be conveniently absent at exactly the right moment, contrary to what the text describes. That's special pleading.

The critical-source explanation is much cleaner. Most scholars working on Numbers — Levine, Milgrom, Knohl — recognize that Numbers 16 is a composite of at least two rebellion stories (the Dathan/Abiram revolt, which is older Yahwist or non-P material, and the Korah revolt, which is a P-style Levitical conflict over priestly prerogatives) that have been redactionally fused. Numbers 26:11 is a Priestly correction-clause inserted to protect the reputation of the Korahite Levitical guild that controlled significant portions of the temple music tradition (Psalms 42, 44-49, 84-85, 87-88 are 'sons of Korah' psalms). The Chronicler relies on the same correction. The contradiction is the seam between source traditions, smoothed over with a single sentence reassuring the reader that the Korahite singers in their own day still had a legitimate genealogy.

The harmonization is possible only if you ignore what the text says about Korah's tent and assume his sons skipped the rebellion. The critical read explains both the contradiction and the redactional motivation. Genuine contradiction with a clear historical fingerprint.

entries.question: Who was Zelophahad's father?
entries.summary: Numbers 27:1 and Joshua 17:3 give Zelophehad's genealogy as Hepher → Gilead → Machir → Manasseh, making Hepher his immediate father. 1 Chronicles 7:14-15 lists Zelophehad as a son of Manasseh directly, with a different intermediate genealogy entirely. The two genealogies disagree about who Zelophehad's father was.
entries.commentary:
The apologetic harmonization here leans on the Hebrew word *ben*, which means 'son' but is also routinely used for 'descendant' or 'grandson.' Archer goes this route: 1 Chronicles is using *ben* loosely to call Zelophehad a 'son' of Manasseh in the broader sense of 'descendant,' even though the immediate father is actually Hepher per Numbers and Joshua. This is a real feature of biblical Hebrew genealogies, and it's not a stupid argument — the same trick is used to handle the 'Christ son of David, son of Abraham' formulation in Matthew 1:1.

But 1 Chronicles 7:14-15 is doing more than just calling Zelophehad a generic descendant. It's a structured genealogy: 'The sons of Manasseh: Asriel... and the second was Zelophehad,' with sister and wife relationships threaded through. The Chronicler is naming two sons of Manasseh in parallel — Asriel and Zelophehad. To rescue this, the apologist has to argue that the Chronicler is calling Zelophehad a 'son' in a sense different from how he's calling Asriel a 'son' in the same sentence. That's not how parallel constructions work.

Worse, the Chronicler's text in 1 Chronicles 7:14-19 is one of the most textually corrupt passages in the Hebrew Bible. The MT is so garbled that virtually every modern critical translation reorders or emends the verses, and the LXX preserves a partially different version. Sara Japhet's commentary on Chronicles devotes pages to untangling it. What we likely have is the Chronicler working with a fragmented or alternative genealogical tradition for Manasseh that doesn't match the Numbers/Joshua tradition, and the redactional history of his sources didn't smooth the conflict. Gary Knoppers' Anchor Bible Chronicles commentary also treats the passage as showing genuine tension with the Pentateuchal genealogy.

The loose-*ben* harmonization works if you assume the Chronicler meant 'descendant' for Zelophehad while meaning 'son' for the other names in the same list. That's inconsistent reading. The cleaner explanation is that two distinct genealogical traditions for the Manassite clans have been preserved without harmonization, and Chronicles knew a tradition that named Zelophehad more directly under Manasseh. Mild but real contradiction. Mostly weak as a 'gotcha,' but it does flag a real source-critical seam.

entries.question: What is the correct recipe for the new moon sacrifice?
entries.summary: Numbers 28:11-15 prescribes the new moon offering as two young bulls, one ram, seven male lambs, and a goat for sin offering. Ezekiel 46:6 prescribes one bull, one ram, and six lambs. Two different sacrificial recipes for the same monthly festival.
entries.commentary:
There's no real apologetic playbook here because the harmonization is so transparently strained. The standard move, found in Lamar Eugene Cooper's NAC Ezekiel and dialed back in Daniel Block's NICOT volume, is that Ezekiel 40-48 describes the future eschatological temple, not the wilderness/Mosaic tabernacle, so the sacrificial recipes don't have to match. Different temple, different rules. That's the strongest version of the harmonization on offer.

But if Ezekiel's temple visions are eschatological, that means God either changed His mind about the proper monthly sacrifice or the original Numbers 28 instruction wasn't actually an eternal ordinance — even though Numbers 28:14 calls it a 'continual burnt offering throughout your generations.' You're trading a contradiction in numbers for a contradiction in permanence. The Jewish tradition felt this acutely. The Babylonian Talmud (b. Shabbat 13b; cf. b. Menahot 45a, b. Hagigah 13a) preserves the famous story that the book of Ezekiel was nearly excluded from the canon because its sacrificial regulations contradicted the Torah, and only Hananiah ben Hezekiah's marathon midnight reading sessions (with three hundred barrels of oil) reconciled them — barely. The rabbis themselves recognized this as a real conflict, not an apparent one.

The critical-scholarship read is much cleaner. Walther Zimmerli's Hermeneia Ezekiel commentary and Daniel Block's NICOT recognize that Ezekiel 40-48 represents a priestly program for temple restoration that diverges from the Pentateuchal sacrificial system in multiple places — not just the new moon offering, but also the Passover, the daily *tamid*, and the role of the *nasi*. Ezekiel's program is an alternative priestly vision developed during the exile, possibly representing a Zadokite faction's idealized blueprint. The Pentateuchal P material was shaped (at least in part) by a different priestly trajectory. They didn't get fully harmonized in the canon.

You can wave at 'eschatological temple' and call it solved, but that just relocates the contradiction without resolving it. Either Numbers 28's eternal ordinance isn't eternal, or Ezekiel's prescription is wrong. Or — much more parsimoniously — these are two priestly traditions in disagreement. Genuine contradiction, well-attested in pre-modern Jewish reception.

entries.question: Did the Israelites kill every male in Midian?
entries.summary: Numbers 31:7 reports the Israelites killed all the males of Midian, and verses 17-18 instruct them to kill every remaining male child plus every non-virgin woman. Yet Judges 6 opens with the Midianites oppressing Israel for seven years, swarming up 'as grasshoppers for multitude.' If every Midianite male was slaughtered in Numbers, where did the Judges 6 horde come from?
entries.commentary:
The apologetic harmonization, articulated by Archer and echoed in basically every conservative commentary on Judges, has two parts. First: Numbers 31 describes the killing of one specific Midianite confederation that was complicit in the Baal-Peor incident, not the whole Midianite people, who lived across a wide region from northwest Arabia to the Sinai. Second: even within that confederation, the population had two centuries to recover before Judges 6, and Midianites in other regions were untouched. The key passage is Numbers 31:9, which says the Israelites took Midianite women and children captive — implying the campaign was localized to a single Midianite military encampment. Archer's version: 'all the males' means 'all the males who showed up to fight.'

This is actually one of the more defensible apologetic harmonizations in the database, because Numbers 31:9 does say women and children were taken captive, which means *some* Midianites survived the campaign — Israelite soldiers married a number of those captives in Numbers 31:18. So the Judges 6 Midianites have to be either descendants of those captives' relatives or a different geographic Midianite group. Susan Niditch in *War in the Hebrew Bible* and Jack Sasson in his Anchor Bible Judges note that 'Midian' in the biblical traditions is a fluid ethnic-geographic label covering multiple distinct groups across centuries.

The rhetoric of Numbers 31:7, though, is the problem. The text says 'they slew all the males' — kol-zakhar, totalizing language. Then verse 17 has Moses ordering the killing of every remaining male child and every non-virgin woman among the captives. The text reads as a complete ethnic erasure of the targeted group. To then have the Midianites swarming Israel as a major military power two centuries later in Judges 6 strains the totalizing rhetoric. Niditch and Lawson Younger's commentaries on Judges both note that the Numbers 31 herem traditions and the Judges 6 oppression don't sit easily together — the Pentateuch tells you Midian was annihilated, the Deuteronomistic History tells you they were a regional power.

The harmonization works partially. 'All the males' can be read as 'all the combatants of one Midianite group,' especially given the explicit captives. But Numbers 31's language is hyperbolically genocidal in a way that doesn't comport with Judges 6's account of a flourishing, expansionist Midianite population. The simplest read is that two different traditions are at work — a Pentateuchal herem story and a Deuteronomistic oppression story — that didn't get harmonized. Mild contradiction, weakened by the captives clause but not eliminated.

entries.question: Was Moses meek?
entries.summary: Numbers 12:3 famously calls Moses 'very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth.' Numbers 31:14-18 has Moses raging at his officers for sparing the Midianite women and personally ordering the slaughter of every male child and every non-virgin Midianite woman. The 'meekest man on earth' description sits awkwardly next to the war-crime episode.
entries.commentary:
The apologetic harmonization, articulated by Archer and echoed across evangelical biblical theologies, depends entirely on redefining 'meek.' Hebrew *anav*, the word in Numbers 12:3, doesn't mean weak or passive — it carries the sense of humble, submissive to God, not asserting personal status. So Moses can be *anav* before Yahweh while still executing harsh judgment when commanded. Meekness is theological humility, not behavioral mildness. That's the cleanest harmonization, and it's lexically defensible. *Anav* and *anavah* in the Psalms are the virtues of the righteous sufferer, not Mister Rogers.

The lexical move is fine. Moses being humble before Yahweh is compatible with Moses being ferocious toward enemies of Yahweh. So far so good. But the contradiction the SAB is poking at isn't really lexical — it's that Numbers 12:3 is a parenthetical authorial comment that reads as obviously self-promotional given that Moses is the alleged author of the Pentateuch. 'Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth' is one of the strongest internal arguments against Mosaic authorship in the entire Pentateuch. Ibn Ezra noticed this in the 12th century and flagged it as one of his discreet hints that Moses didn't write the whole book. Spinoza turned the same observation into a Mosaic-authorship-killer in the *Tractatus Theologico-Politicus*.

The critical view: Numbers 12:3 is a Priestly or post-Priestly editorial gloss inserted to defend Moses' character against the murmuring of Aaron and Miriam in the surrounding narrative. The wider Numbers material then preserves a much messier portrait of Moses — angry strikes on the rock (Numbers 20), commanding ethnic-cleansing campaigns (Numbers 31), reacting violently to apostasy (Exodus 32, where he orders Levite massacres). Whoever wrote 12:3 had a specific apologetic agenda about Moses' character that doesn't map cleanly onto the rest of the corpus.

So the harmonization works at the lexical level (anav doesn't mean nonviolent), but it doesn't really address the surface contradiction the question is pointing to. You can rescue 'meek' theologically while still admitting that 'meekest man on earth' sits awkwardly with 'kill every male child.' The contradiction reads as forced once you understand the Hebrew, but it survives as a genuine literary tension. Weak as a hard contradiction, real as a literary observation.

entries.question: Who survived to see the promised land during the Exodus?
entries.summary: Numbers 14:22-24 has Yahweh swear that none of the rebellious generation will see the promised land 'but my servant Caleb' — singular. Numbers 14:37-38, 26:64-65, and 32:10-12 all explicitly include Joshua alongside Caleb as the two survivors. The first passage names only Caleb; the surrounding passages name both Caleb and Joshua.
entries.commentary:
The apologetic harmonization is reasonable: Numbers 14:24 is the focal point of God's first speech, naming Caleb specifically because of Caleb's distinctive faithful report. Joshua's exemption is then formalized in the surrounding verses. The passages aren't contradictory; they're cumulative — Caleb's exemption is announced first, Joshua's gets specified shortly after. Archer takes this line. Wenham's Tyndale Numbers and Cole's NAC volume both treat verse 24 as a focused naming of the most demonstrative loyalist, not a comprehensive list of exempted persons.

This is actually one of the better apologetic harmonizations because the narrative flow does support it. Numbers 14 is one continuous scene: the spies' report (chap 13), the people's rebellion (14:1-10), Moses' intercession (14:11-19), Yahweh's verdict (14:20-35), the spies' deaths (14:36-38). Joshua is named in verses 6 and 30 of the same chapter as one of the faithful spies. So when verse 24 highlights Caleb only, it's reasonable to read this as rhetorical focus rather than systematic exclusion of Joshua. The surrounding context unambiguously includes Joshua.

But there's a redactional pattern here that the apologetic read overlooks. Numbers 14:24 is structured as a self-contained divine oath — 'I will bring him into the land...and his seed shall possess it' — with no reference to Joshua. Levine's Anchor Bible Numbers and Knierim & Coats' FOTL volume both note that the Caleb traditions in Numbers 13-14 and Joshua 14 represent an originally independent Calebite tradition that was later harmonized with the Joshua tradition. Caleb is a Kenizzite, not technically an Israelite, and the Calebite clan claims to Hebron in Joshua 14:13-14 are an independent settlement narrative. Joshua's parallel exemption appears to be a secondary insertion, smoothing the older Caleb-only oath into the Joshua-led conquest narrative.

So the surface contradiction is mild. The text as it stands names both. But the tension verse 24 creates is a fingerprint of an older Caleb-only tradition partially overwritten by the Joshua editorial layer. The apologist harmonization works narratively. The critical reading explains why verse 24 reads the way it does. Weak as a stand-alone contradiction, real as evidence of textual layering.

entries.question: How long does God's anger last?
entries.books_in_tension: Numbers, Psalms, Jeremiah, Micah, Malachi, Judith, Matthew
entries.summary: The Bible gives at least four mutually incompatible answers about the duration of God's anger. Judith 8:15 says God doesn't get angry at all. Psalm 30:5 says His anger lasts only a moment. Numbers 32:13, Psalm 103:9, Jeremiah 3:12, and Micah 7:18 say His anger doesn't last forever (but sometimes for forty years). Jeremiah 17:4, Malachi 1:4, and Matthew 25:41-46 say His anger and punishment burn forever.
entries.commentary:
Apologists typically handle this with a context-dependent harmonization: God's anger is short toward His covenant people who repent (Psalm 30:5, Micah 7:18), longer when corporate judgment is required (Numbers 32:13's forty years), and eternal toward the unrepentant or toward the cursed (Matthew 25:41). Different durations apply to different recipients. Geisler & Howe and Walton's *NIV Application Commentary* both go this direction. Daniel Block, in his Judges/Ruth NAC, articulates a version of this for Old Testament wrath language: corporate judgment is bounded; covenantal anger toward Israel never permanent; eschatological wrath toward the unrepentant terminal. That's a reasonable systematic theology framework.

The framework can paper over most of the duration verses, but it has real cracks. Judith 8:15 — admittedly a deuterocanonical text — flatly says God 'will not threaten as a man, nor be inflamed to anger as a son of man,' which sits in obvious tension with the dozens of biblical passages where Yahweh's anger flares against Israel, against individuals, against the nations. The 'not inflamed to anger' line in Judith reflects a Hellenistic-Jewish philosophical tradition (apatheia, divine impassibility) that's at odds with the older Hebrew conception of *aph-Yahweh* — the burning nostril of God. Brueggemann, Heschel, and Crenshaw all describe this tension as inherent to the development of the biblical concept of God: an older anthropomorphic deity whose anger is a real emotional flare, gradually rephilosophized into an immutable being whose 'wrath' becomes a metaphor for judicial action.

More importantly, Jeremiah's own corpus contradicts itself directly. Jeremiah 3:12 says God will not keep anger forever; Jeremiah 17:4 says the fire kindled in His anger will burn forever. You can rescue this with the audience-distinction move (3:12 addresses returning Israel, 17:4 addresses Judah's apostasy), but you've still got the same prophet using identical language about Yahweh's *aph* with diametrically opposed durations. William Holladay's Hermeneia Jeremiah and Jack Lundbom's Anchor Bible Jeremiah both treat these as products of different redactional layers — the optimistic-restoration material vs. the unrelenting-judgment material.

The apologetic systematization works as a theological framework but only by stitching together verses that reflect very different theological worldviews — Hebrew anthropopathism, Hellenistic impassibility, prophetic restoration theology, apocalyptic eternal judgment. The Bible doesn't speak with one voice on this. Genuine contradiction at the textual level, smoothable only with substantial harmonizing scaffolding.

entries.question: How should the Moabites be treated?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 2:9 has Yahweh forbid Israel from picking a fight with Moab or seizing Moabite land, because Yahweh assigned Ar to the descendants of Lot. Judges 3:28-30 has Israel slaughter ten thousand Moabites and subdue Moab as a tributary, and Jeremiah 48:2 calls for the destruction of Moab as a nation. The peace-with-Moab and destroy-Moab traditions don't coordinate.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic move, found in Block's NAC Judges, Ruth and echoed across evangelical commentaries, is to read Deuteronomy 2:9 as a one-time wilderness travel policy and Judges 3 / Jeremiah 48 as later judgments triggered by Moabite aggression against Israel. Eglon attacks Israel first in Judges 3, so Ehud's response is defensive war, not unprovoked conquest. Jeremiah 48 is a prophetic oracle of judgment for Moab's idolatry and pride. Neither violates Deuteronomy 2:9, because both come centuries later under different circumstances. That's the harmonization, and it's not absurd.

The problem is the rhetorical totality of the later passages. Deuteronomy 2:9 isn't framed as a temporary travel courtesy — it's framed as a divine land grant: 'I will not give you any of their land for a possession, because I have given Ar to the children of Lot for a possession.' The language is permanent. Then Jeremiah 48:2 has Yahweh declaring 'Come, and let us cut it off from being a nation' — direct reversal of the Deuteronomic land grant. Lawson Younger's NIVAC Judges and Robert Carroll's OTL Jeremiah both observe that the prophets' oracles against Moab assume a posture toward Moab that's irreconcilable with the Deuteronomic protection.

The critical-scholarship explanation involves recognizing that the Hebrew Bible preserves multiple memory traditions about Moab. The Deuteronomic 'kinship' tradition treats Moab as Lot's descendants, fellow Abrahamic relatives whose territory is divinely protected. The Deuteronomistic History (Judges, Samuel, Kings) treats Moab as a regional rival in cycles of conflict and tribute. The classical prophets treat Moab as a target of eschatological judgment alongside the other nations. These traditions reflect different historical periods and theological agendas. Moshe Weinfeld has written about how 'Moabite' identity in biblical discourse is highly variable depending on the era and the theological purposes of the writer.

The harmonization works at a chronological-narrative level — Deuteronomy 2 was the wilderness era, Judges 3 was post-conquest, Jeremiah 48 was the late monarchy. But the absolute land-grant language in Deuteronomy 2:9 ('I have given Ar to the children of Lot for a possession') doesn't expire. Either Yahweh's gift to Lot's descendants is irrevocable (and Jeremiah 48 contradicts it) or it isn't (and Deuteronomy 2:9 misrepresents Yahweh's actual policy). The cleaner explanation is that these are traditions in tension, smoothed by sequential reading. Mild but real contradiction.

entries.question: How should the Ammonites be treated?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 2:19 and 2:37 forbid Israel from invading or seizing Ammonite land, because Yahweh assigned that land to the descendants of Lot. Judges 11:32 has Jephthah pass over to fight the Ammonites and slaughter them, and Jeremiah 49:2 has Yahweh promising Rabbah will become 'a desolate heap, and her daughters shall be burned with fire.' The Ammonite protection clause and the destroy-Ammon oracles can't both stand at face value.
entries.commentary:
The apologetic harmonization parallels the Moabite case. Deuteronomy 2:19 is a one-time wilderness travel directive; Judges 11 and Jeremiah 49 are later responses to Ammonite aggression. Jephthah's war is defensive — Ammon attacks Israel first, claiming territorial rights east of the Jordan. Jeremiah's oracle is judicial response to Ammon's idolatry and territorial encroachment after the fall of Israel. Block and Younger handle it this way and the chronological framework does cover most of the surface tension.

But the structure of the Deuteronomic passage is identical to the Moabite case: Yahweh declares the land 'has been given to the children of Lot for a possession' — the same permanent-grant language. Jeremiah 49:1 directly attacks this premise, asking, 'Has Israel no sons? Has he no heir? Why then has Milcom dispossessed Gad?' — implying that the children of Lot have *no* legitimate claim to the land. This isn't just a punishment for Ammonite misbehavior; it's a reversal of the Deuteronomic land theology. Jack Lundbom and William Holladay both flag this tension in their commentaries on Jeremiah 49.

The critical-scholarship reading is the same as for Moab. Two traditions about Ammon coexist in the Hebrew Bible: a 'Lot's descendants' tradition that treats them as protected kin, and a 'enemy nation' tradition that subjects them to herem-style judgment. These traditions reflect different periods and theological frameworks. The Deuteronomic protective stance probably reflects a period when relations with Ammon were stable; the prophetic oracles reflect later periods of conflict. The Hebrew Bible's varied stance toward the Trans-Jordanian neighbors reflects the same kind of multi-tradition layering observed across other ethnic-relations material.

The harmonization patches the surface narrative if you grant that Yahweh's land grants are revocable based on the recipients' conduct. But the Deuteronomic text doesn't include any such conditions — it's an unconditional 'I have given' clause. To invalidate it later requires the kind of theological revision that the prophets actually do in Jeremiah 49:1 ('Has Israel no heir?'). The text shows the seam. Mild contradiction with a clear redactional fingerprint.

entries.question: Will the earth last forever?
entries.books_in_tension: Deuteronomy, Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, Hebrews, 2 Peter, Revelation
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 4:40, Psalm 37:29, Psalm 78:69, Psalm 104:5, and Ecclesiastes 1:4 all assert that the earth abides forever — Psalm 104:5 specifically says it 'should not be removed for ever.' Psalm 102:25-26, Isaiah 65:17, the Synoptic apocalyptic discourses (Matthew 24:35 and parallels), Hebrews 1:10-11, 2 Peter 3:10-13, and Revelation 21:1 say the earth will perish, melt, pass away, or be replaced by a new earth. The everlasting-earth and perishing-earth traditions are in direct tension.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization, articulated clearly in Geisler & Howe and developed in Wayne Grudem's *Systematic Theology*, distinguishes between 'forever' as 'for an extremely long time / for the duration of the present age' versus 'forever' as 'truly eternal.' On this read, when Ecclesiastes says the earth abides forever, it means for the foreseeable future, not absolute eternity. The 'forever' verses describe the present cosmos's relative stability against human transience; the eschatological verses describe the eventual transformation. Grudem additionally argues, and many evangelical eschatologists agree, that the 'new earth' in 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 21 is a *renewed* earth, not a destroyed-and-replaced earth — the earth abides, just transformed. That's the strongest harmonization on offer.

The problem is the Hebrew word *olam* (forever) doesn't actually carry that English-style ambiguity in the contexts where it's used in Psalm 104:5 and Ecclesiastes 1:4. *Olam* in these wisdom-poetic contexts means 'permanent, of indefinite duration, not subject to change.' Ecclesiastes 1:4 is making a contrast between human generational mortality and the earth's stability — the rhetorical force depends on the earth being genuinely permanent in contrast to mortal humans. If you reduce *olam* to 'a long time,' the verse loses its point. Choon-Leong Seow's Anchor Bible Ecclesiastes commentary makes exactly this argument: Qoheleth's pessimism about human transience is anchored in the perceived absolute permanence of the cosmic order.

The 'renewed earth' apologetic for 2 Peter 3 is also contradicted by 2 Peter 3:10's actual language. *Stoicheia luthēsetai*, 'the elements will be dissolved,' and *katakaēsetai*, 'will be burned up' (with significant textual variants reading 'will be discovered' instead — a known problem in 2 Peter textual criticism, see Bauckham's WBC), describe destruction, not refurbishment. Revelation 21:1 says explicitly 'the first heaven and the first earth had passed away' — *apēlthon*, the same verb used for the abolition of the old order. Richard Bauckham's WBC 2 Peter and David Aune's WBC Revelation both read these passages as describing genuine cosmic dissolution, not just renewal.

More importantly, the contradiction reflects a real theological development. The older Israelite cosmological view in Psalm 104 and Ecclesiastes — earth-as-permanent-foundation — is a creation-theology framework. The apocalyptic destruction-and-replacement view in Daniel, 2 Peter, Revelation, and the Synoptic Apocalypse is a later theological framework, influenced by Iranian and Hellenistic apocalyptic traditions. John Collins' *Apocalyptic Imagination* tracks exactly this shift. The two cosmologies don't fully harmonize. The apologist position requires either 'forever' to mean 'temporary' or 'destroyed' to mean 'renewed.' Either way, you're redefining ordinary language to rescue the harmonization. Genuine contradiction reflecting two distinct theological eras.

entries.question: Did the Israelites see God face to face on Mount Horeb?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 5:2-4 says Yahweh spoke to the Israelites at Horeb 'face to face out of the midst of the fire.' Deuteronomy 4:12, two chapters earlier in the same book, says they 'heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice.' Same author, same event, same book — different claims about whether the Israelites visually perceived Yahweh.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization, articulated by Tigay in the JPS Deuteronomy and gestured at in Block's NIVAC, is to read 'face to face' (*panim be-panim*) as an idiom meaning 'directly, in immediate communication' rather than as a description of literal visual encounter. The phrase is used elsewhere — Genesis 32:30, Numbers 14:14, Exodus 33:11 — sometimes with clear visual content and sometimes as a metaphor for direct, intimate address. So Deuteronomy 5:4 means 'directly addressed,' compatible with Deuteronomy 4:12's 'no form, only a voice.' That's the strongest harmonization, and it's lexically defensible.

The problem is the *panim be-panim* idiom isn't always non-visual. Exodus 33:11 says Yahweh spoke to Moses *panim el panim*, just as a man speaks to his friend — but in that same chapter, just verses later, Yahweh says 'no man can see my face and live' (33:20), and Moses gets to see only Yahweh's *back*. The idiom in Exodus 33 explicitly has both a metaphorical sense (intimate communication) and a visual sense (what Moses can or cannot actually see). Deuteronomy 5:4 specifies 'face to face *in the mountain out of the midst of the fire*' — the visual setting is part of the description. Brevard Childs and Moshe Weinfeld both note that Deuteronomy 5:4 is reading the Sinai/Horeb encounter as an unmediated experience, while 4:12 is reading it as mediated entirely through voice without form.

The critical-scholarship explanation is direct. Deuteronomy 4 and Deuteronomy 5 reflect different theological agendas inside the Deuteronomic corpus. Deuteronomy 4 is part of a later theological framework — Weinfeld places it in the late Deuteronomistic redaction — that aggressively polices against any visual representation of Yahweh, in line with the Deuteronomic anti-iconic theology. The 'no form, only a voice' framing is a deliberate de-visualization of the Sinai encounter to support the prohibition of images later in the chapter (4:15-19). Deuteronomy 5 preserves the older, more anthropomorphic 'face-to-face' tradition that the chapter 4 redactor was trying to neutralize. Two layers, two theological positions, side by side in the same book.

The idiomatic harmonization is partially defensible. *Panim be-panim* can mean direct address. But the addition of 'in the mountain out of the midst of the fire' weights the description toward genuine encounter. Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer have both written about how the Hebrew Bible preserves competing traditions about whether Yahweh has visible form, and Deuteronomy 4 vs. 5 is a textbook example. Mild contradiction at the surface level, well-attested as a redactional seam in critical scholarship.

entries.question: Are the laws of the Old Testament still binding?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 7:9, 11:1, 12:1, and Psalm 119:151-160 declare the commandments and statutes binding 'forever,' 'always,' and 'to a thousand generations.' Jesus in Matthew 22:37-40 collapses the entire Law into two commandments. Luke 16:16 has Jesus say the Law and the prophets were only until John the Baptist. Either the Mosaic Law is permanently binding or it has been superseded.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization runs along familiar Reformed and dispensationalist lines, and Walter Kaiser's *Toward Old Testament Ethics* articulates it well. The Old Testament commandments are categorized into moral, civil, and ceremonial, with only the moral law binding on Christians; the civil and ceremonial laws were always provisional, fulfilled in Christ. Matthew 22:37-40 doesn't abolish the Law, it summarizes it — Jesus is identifying the two greatest commandments around which all the others organize. Luke 16:16 is read as describing a transition point in salvation history: the Law and Prophets gave way to the kingdom announcement, but the moral content of the Law continues. So 'forever' applies to the moral law, while the ceremonial law was always meant to expire. That's a sophisticated harmonization with a long pedigree.

The problem is that the Pentateuch and the post-exilic texts that endorse it don't operate with a moral/civil/ceremonial trichotomy. That distinction is a Christian theological construction (Aquinas formalized it) that allows you to retain Sabbath law as a 'principle' while ditching dietary regulations as 'ceremony.' E. P. Sanders' *Paul, the Law, and the Jewish People* and James Dunn's *The New Perspective on Paul* both demolished the assumption that ancient Jews categorized Torah obligations this way. To Deuteronomy 11:1, 'his charge, his statutes, his judgments, and his commandments' are all to be kept — there's no internal sorting mechanism for which subset is permanent.

Luke 16:16 is also harder to harmonize than the apologetic move suggests. The text reads: 'The law and the prophets were until John; since then the gospel of the kingdom has been preached.' The natural sense is dispensational displacement: a previous era ended, a new one began. Joseph Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible Luke argues that Luke is here articulating a clear two-stage salvation history in which the Law's primary function gives way to the kingdom proclamation. Matthew, by contrast, presents Jesus as saying not one jot or tittle will pass from the Law (Matthew 5:18) — a position in considerable tension with Luke 16:16. Ulrich Luz's Hermeneia Matthew commentary and François Bovon's Hermeneia Luke commentary both note the divergent positions on the Law within the New Testament canon itself.

The two-commandment summary is the most defensible harmonization. Jesus genuinely is summarizing rather than abolishing. But Luke 16:16 reads as an explicit dispensational shift, and Paul's letters (Galatians 3:23-25) make explicit that the Law was a 'pedagogue' that has been displaced. The New Testament itself preserves multiple positions on the Law's continuing binding force. Once you stack that against the Old Testament's repeated 'forever' language, the contradiction is structural. Genuine, with the surface tension only resolvable by importing a later Christian theological framework that the Old Testament writers wouldn't recognize.

entries.question: Does God know what is in everyone's heart?
entries.summary: Acts 1:24, Psalm 44:21, and Psalm 139:2-3 affirm that God knows the secrets of the heart, that He understands thoughts from afar, that nothing in human consciousness is hidden from Him. But Deuteronomy 8:2, 13:3, and 2 Chronicles 32:31 describe God testing or 'proving' people specifically *to know* what is in their hearts — implying He didn't already know. Either God is omniscient about human hearts or He uses tests to learn what's in them.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization, articulated cleanly in Wayne Grudem's *Systematic Theology* and developed in Bruce Ware's work on classical theism, distinguishes between God's exhaustive knowledge and the *demonstration* or *manifestation* of what He already knows. God doesn't test Israel because He needs information — He tests them so that *Israel* will know what's in their own hearts, or so that the testing manifests in history what is already eternally known to God. The 'to know' language in Deuteronomy is anthropomorphic accommodation, the way scripture often speaks of God in human terms. That's the strongest harmonization, and it's been the standard answer since Augustine.

The problem is the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 8:2 doesn't really support the anthropomorphic-accommodation read on its own terms. The verb is *la-da'at*, the infinitive of 'to know' with the explicit purpose particle — 'in order to know.' Tigay's JPS Deuteronomy notes that the natural reading is that the testing serves an epistemological function for Yahweh, and that the older Hebrew theology represented in the older strata of the Pentateuch did not assume the kind of exhaustive, eternal omniscience that later Hellenistic-Jewish and Christian theology developed. Genesis 18:21 has Yahweh saying 'I will go down now, and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry of it, which is come unto me; and if not, I will know' — same epistemological language. Genesis 22:12 has the angel of Yahweh tell Abraham 'now I know that you fear God,' after the Akedah test. The pattern is consistent.

Mark Smith and Benjamin Sommer have written extensively about how the early Israelite deity is conceptualized as embodied, anthropomorphic, and spatially located in ways that don't fit the philosophically perfect God of later theology. Yahweh in older texts walks in the garden 'in the cool of the day' (Genesis 3:8) and comes down to investigate (Genesis 18, Genesis 11 for Babel); Tigay, Brueggemann, and Crenshaw extend this to the epistemic side — Yahweh uses tests to gain knowledge. The omniscience-affirming verses — Psalm 139, Acts 1:24 — reflect a more developed theology, often in poetic-hymnic or post-exilic contexts where the philosophical conception of God has matured. The contradiction is between two strata of biblical theology, not just between two surface verses.

The accommodation argument works only if you assume the doctrine of omniscience was already in place when Deuteronomy 8 was written and the writer was using metaphor. The critical view is the reverse: omniscience is a later development, and Deuteronomy 8 means what it says. James Crenshaw's *A Whirlpool of Torment* and Walter Brueggemann's *Theology of the Old Testament* both treat this kind of internal tension as evidence of theological development across the canon. Genuine contradiction with deep theological roots.

entries.question: Are we all God's children?
entries.books_in_tension: Deuteronomy, Psalms, Hosea, Matthew, Luke, John, Acts, Galatians
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 14:1 calls all Israel 'the children of the LORD your God.' Psalm 82:6 declares 'all of you are children of the most High.' Hosea 1:10, Acts 17:29, and Jesus' teaching of the Lord's Prayer all use universal-sounding 'Father' / 'children' language. But Galatians 3:26 says you become children of God 'by faith in Christ Jesus' — implying that without that faith, you aren't. Either everyone is already God's child by virtue of creation/covenant, or only believers are God's children by faith.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization, articulated across Pauline biblical theology, distinguishes between two senses of divine sonship. There's a creation-sense (everyone is God's offspring as a created being, per Acts 17:29) and a covenant/adoptive sense (some are God's children in the soteriologically loaded sense of being heirs and adopted into the family). Deuteronomy and the Psalms operate with the first sense; Paul in Galatians 3:26 operates with the second. The categories don't conflict; they're different layers of relationship. That's the strongest harmonization, and N. T. Wright develops it well in *Paul and the Faithfulness of God*; James Scott's *Adoption as Sons of God* (WUNT 2/48, Mohr, 1992) gives the more granular case for *huiothesia* as a Pauline-specific category distinct from generic creation-sonship.

This is one of the better apologetic harmonizations in the database, because it tracks a real distinction in biblical usage. Acts 17:29 in Paul's Areopagus speech does invoke Stoic-flavored creation language ('we are God's offspring,' citing Aratus), and that's clearly a different mode of sonship than what he means in Galatians. James Dunn's BNTC Galatians and Hans Dieter Betz's Hermeneia Galatians both treat 3:26 as part of a specific argumentative thread about Abrahamic descent and inclusion in the people of God through Christ — not a denial that creation includes all humans as creatures of God.

But the Galatians passage and its surrounding logic do generate a real tension with the older texts. Psalm 82:6, in its original Hebrew Bible context, isn't using fictive-kinship language — it's a divine-council passage in which Yahweh is judging the lesser elohim and calling them 'sons of the Most High.' Mark Smith and others read it as residual polytheism. When Jesus uses the verse in John 10:34 to defend himself against blasphemy charges, He's reapplying it to humans, expanding the sonship reach. So we already have multiple competing senses of 'son of God' across the canon: divine-council members, all Israel, all faithful Israel, all humanity (as creatures), specifically those who have faith in Christ. The phrase doesn't have a stable referent.

The creation-sense vs. faith-adoption-sense distinction is theologically clean but it doesn't fully neutralize the Hebrew Bible's universal language about Israel. Deuteronomy 14:1's 'you are children of the LORD your God' is addressed to all Israel by virtue of covenant membership, not by virtue of individual faith. Galatians 3:26's 'children of God by faith' specifically excludes anyone outside that faith — including unbelieving ethnic Israel. Paul's argument *requires* a redefinition of who counts as God's children, which is why Romans 9-11 gets complicated. The harmonization works at a systematic-theology level but obscures that Paul was reframing the relationship in a way that the older texts didn't anticipate. Mild contradiction, mostly resolvable by recognizing distinct senses, with residual tension over what counts as authoritative sonship.

entries.question: Were the Israelites to spare the trees in the countries they invaded?
entries.summary: Deuteronomy 20:19 prohibits destroying fruit trees during a siege: 'thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them.' 2 Kings 3:19 has the prophet Elisha instruct Israel to do exactly that against Moab — 'fell every good tree, and stop all wells of water, and mar every good piece of land with stones.' Either the Deuteronomic prohibition is binding or Elisha's instructions to Israel through Yahweh's prophet override it.
entries.commentary:
The standard apologetic harmonization runs along two lines. First (Archer, Walter Kaiser): Deuteronomy 20:19 only prohibits destruction of *fruit* trees specifically (Hebrew *etz ma'akhal*, food trees), and the 2 Kings 3:19 instruction is to destroy 'every good tree' in a more general sense — possibly non-fruit-bearing trees that contribute to the enemy's military or strategic position. Second: 2 Kings 3 is a special divine command for a specific situation (the Moabite war), and special divine commands can override general statutes when Yahweh authorizes it. Most evangelical harmonizers go with some combination of the two. T. R. Hobbs in his WBC 2 Kings volume softens the contradiction this way.

The first move runs into the Hebrew. Deuteronomy 20:20 actually allows the cutting of non-fruit trees — 'Only the trees which thou knowest that they be not trees for meat, thou shalt destroy and cut them down' — for siege works. So the Deuteronomic statute already distinguishes between fruit trees (preserved) and non-fruit trees (allowable for siege). 2 Kings 3:19's instruction to fell 'every good tree' (*kol-etz tov*) doesn't easily restrict to non-fruit trees — *tov* in agricultural contexts typically modifies productive trees. Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor's Anchor Bible 2 Kings note that the language of 2 Kings 3:19, combined with stopping all wells and ruining every good piece of land with stones, describes a comprehensive scorched-earth campaign — an ecological war crime by Deuteronomic standards.

The second harmonization (special command override) is more honest, but it concedes the surface contradiction. If Yahweh through Elisha commands Israel to do what Deuteronomy forbids, then either the Deuteronomic statute isn't actually permanent (which contradicts its own claims to lasting validity) or Yahweh's commands are inconsistent across time. The 'special command' move is a tacit admission that the texts disagree at face value and you need a meta-rule (divine prerogative to override statute) to harmonize them.

The critical-scholarship read is cleaner. Susan Niditch points out that Deuteronomy 20:19's eco-ethical prohibition reflects a developed humanitarian war-ethic in Deuteronomic theology that wasn't shared by the older prophetic narratives. The 2 Kings 3 narrative belongs to the older Elisha cycle, where prophetic authority and divine warfare don't conform to Deuteronomic restrictions. Marvin Sweeney's OTL I & II Kings has also flagged this as one of the places the Deuteronomistic editors didn't fully harmonize their source material with their statutory program. The contradiction is real and reflects the layering of Israelite war ethics across centuries. Mild but genuine.

answers.answer_explanation: When thou shalt besiege a city a long time, in making war against it to take it, thou shalt not destroy the trees. Deuteronomy 20:19
And ye shall smite every fenced city, and every choice city, and shall fell every good tree. 2 Kings 3:19

assessment.reasoning: Deut 20:19's fruit-tree protection conflicts at face value with Elisha's scorched-earth command in 2 Kings 3:19 (Cogan-Tadmor, Niditch, Sweeney noting unharmonized Deuteronomistic source layering), though the special-divine-command override keeps it from being judged fully unresolvable by all scholars.
